calculating-k-s1.title: Three equilibrium mixtures of H₂, I₂ and HI
calculating-k-s1.text: Three sealed flasks at 450 °C each start with different amounts of H2, I2 and HI and are left to reach equilibrium: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). The table gives the equilibrium concentrations.

calculating-k-s2.title: Nitrosyl chloride decomposing
calculating-k-s2.text: A student puts 0.500 mol of NOCl gas into an empty, sealed 2.00 L flask and holds it at a constant temperature: 2 NOCl(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g) + Cl2(g). When equilibrium is reached, the flask contains 0.0400 mol of Cl2.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> from the data for trial 1.

mistakes.why: Value: [HI] is squared in K, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you doubled [HI] instead of squaring it. Coefficients become exponents.
Value: you inverted K. Products go on top.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> from the data for trial 3.

mistakes.why: Value: [HI] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.

items.q: What do the three trials show about K<sub>c</sub>?
options: K<sub>c</sub> is about the same in each trial.
K<sub>c</sub> is largest in the trial with the most HI.
K<sub>c</sub> depends on which substances were put into the flask first.
K<sub>c</sub> is the same because [H<sub>2</sub>] equals [I<sub>2</sub>] in each trial.

why.correct: At one temperature, every equilibrium mixture of the same reaction gives the same value of K, whatever amounts it started with. Small differences come from measurement precision.
options: Right: K comes out at about 50 every time (50.2, 49.9, 50.0), though the mixtures look nothing alike.
K is a ratio. Trial 3 has the most HI but also more H₂ and I₂ in the right proportions, so K is about the same.
All three started differently, yet K is about the same. At a fixed temperature, K does not depend on the starting mixture.
[H₂] equals [I₂] only in trial 2. K is constant anyway.

items.q: A fourth flask at 450 °C has [H<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0050 M, [I<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0050 M and [HI] = 0.0500 M. Based on the trials, what will happen?
options: HI breaks down, because Q = 100 is greater than K.
More HI forms, because Q = 100 is greater than K.
Nothing, because K changes to match the new mixture.
More HI forms, because [HI] is ten times [H<sub>2</sub>].

why.correct: Use K from the trials (about 50.0). Q = 100 > K, so the net reverse reaction makes H₂ and I₂ until Q = K.
options: Right: Q = (0.0500)² / (0.0050 × 0.0050) = 100, twice K (about 50), so the net reaction goes in reverse.
Q > K means too much product, so HI must break down, not form.
K is fixed at a given temperature; the mixture changes to match K.
Direction comes from comparing Q with K. A large [HI] relative to [H₂] actually makes Q large.

items.q: Calculate the initial concentration of NOCl.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied moles by volume. Molarity is moles divided by liters.
Value: NOCl falls by 2x, not x. Two NOCl react for every Cl₂ that forms.
Value: that is the amount in moles. Divide by the 2.00 L volume to get molarity.

items.q: Use your equilibrium concentrations to calculate K<sub>c</sub> for the decomposition of NOCl at this temperature.

mistakes.why: Value: you used moles instead of concentrations. Divide each amount by 2.00 L first.
Value: [NO] and [NOCl] must be squared, because both have the coefficient 2.
Value: check the changes. NO rises by 2x and NOCl falls by 2x, where x = [Cl₂].

items.q: Put the steps for finding K<sub>c</sub> in this experiment in order.
options: Convert the moles of NOCl and of Cl<sub>2</sub> to molarities.
Write the ICE table with the change row as −2x, +2x and +x.
Set x equal to the equilibrium [Cl<sub>2</sub>] and fill in the equilibrium row.
Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the expression for K<sub>c</sub>.

why.correct: Concentrations first; then the ICE table links the one measured value to every other species through the coefficients; then substitute.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g) at a certain temperature, the equilibrium partial pressures are N<sub>2</sub> 0.50 atm, H<sub>2</sub> 1.5 atm and NH<sub>3</sub> 0.12 atm. Calculate K<sub>p</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: P(H₂) must be cubed, because its coefficient is 3.
Value: raise each pressure to the power of its coefficient.

items.q: Solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS is sealed in an evacuated flask: NH<sub>4</sub>HS(s) ⇌ NH<sub>3</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>S(g). At equilibrium, [NH<sub>3</sub>] = [H<sub>2</sub>S] = 0.0150 M, and 2.00 g of solid remains. Calculate K<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: the solid does not belong in K. Its mass (or amount) never enters the expression.
Value: K is the product of both gas concentrations: [NH₃][H₂S].

why.correct: The solid is left out: K<sub>c</sub> = [NH₃][H₂S] = (0.0150)(0.0150) = 2.25 × 10⁻⁴.

items.q: In the NH<sub>4</sub>HS flask, more solid NH<sub>4</sub>HS is added at constant temperature. What happens to [NH<sub>3</sub>]?
options: It stays the same: the solid is not in Q or K.
It increases, because there is more solid to decompose.
It decreases, because the solid absorbs some NH<sub>3</sub>.
It increases until the gas pressure equals the mass of solid.

why.correct: Pure solids are left out of K and Q because their concentration is fixed. As long as some solid is present, the gas concentrations at equilibrium do not depend on how much solid there is.
options: Right: adding solid leaves Q = [NH₃][H₂S] unchanged, so Q still equals K and there is no shift.
The amount of a pure solid does not change its "concentration", so it does not change Q. Nothing shifts.
The reverse reaction is set by [NH₃][H₂S], which have not changed, so there is no net reaction.
Pressure and mass are not compared like this. The gas concentrations are fixed by K alone.

items.q: Which reaction is a heterogeneous equilibrium?
options: C(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g)
N<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g)
2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g)
Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + SCN<sup>−</sup>(aq) ⇌ FeSCN<sup>2+</sup>(aq)

why.correct: A heterogeneous equilibrium involves species in more than one phase, such as a solid and gases. Its K leaves out the solid.
options: Right: a solid and gases, two phases.
All gases: one phase, a homogeneous equilibrium.
All gases: homogeneous.
All dissolved in one solution: homogeneous.

items.q: A 1.00 L flask starts with 0.200 M CO and 0.200 M H<sub>2</sub>O: CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g). At equilibrium, [CO<sub>2</sub>] = 0.120 M. Calculate K<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the initial concentrations of CO and H₂O. Use the equilibrium ones: 0.200 − 0.120 = 0.080 M.

items.q: A student finds K<sub>c</sub> from the initial concentrations of a reaction mixture instead of the equilibrium ones. Why is the result wrong?
options: K needs equilibrium values; initial ones give Q.
Initial concentrations have too few significant figures.
K needs moles, and concentrations are in molarity.
The initial concentrations should be squared before they are used.

why.correct: K is defined for the equilibrium mixture. Starting concentrations give the value of Q at time zero; the system then changes until Q = K.
options: Right: only equilibrium values give the constant. Starting values give the reaction quotient at the start.
Precision is not the issue. Initial values describe a different state of the system.
K<sub>c</sub> is defined with molar concentrations, so molarity is correct.
Exponents come from coefficients and apply to equilibrium values. Squaring initial values does not fix the problem.

items.q: For A(g) ⇌ 2 B(g), a flask starts with 0.40 M A. At equilibrium [B] = 0.20 M. Which ICE table row is correct for the equilibrium concentrations?

why.correct: Change row: A −x, B +2x. 2x = 0.20 M gives x = 0.10 M. Equilibrium [A] = 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 M.
options: Right: B rose by 2x = 0.20 M, so x = 0.10 M and A fell to 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 M.
This subtracts the change in B directly from A. A falls by x, which is half of B’s rise.
A reversible reaction does not use up its reactant; A remains at equilibrium.
A cannot stay at its starting value while B forms; B is made from A.
